title: López pleads guilty to DUI charge in DC, deal could see charge eventually dropped
summary: Human Services Secretary Rafael López had already "taken full responsibility” when charged with DUI in Washington in January. He made it official Monday, pleading guilty in D.C. Superior Court in a deal that could get the charge dismissed in a year.
content:
by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters December 1, 2025

by Danielle J. Brown, Maryland Matters December 1, 2025

Human Services Secretary Rafael López had already “taken full responsibility” when he was charged with driving under the influence earlier this year in Washington, D.C. He made it official Monday, pleading guilty in D.C. Superior Court in a deal that could get the charge dismissed a year from now.

“I have accepted responsibility and am accountable for my actions,” López said in a written statement Monday. “On the advice of counsel, I will not comment further on legal proceedings at this time. I appreciate the support I have received from family, friends, and colleagues.”

In January, a “Ralph Lopez” was charged in Washington, D.C., with driving under the influence and operating a vehicle while intoxicated. That individual was revealed to be López, Maryland’s secretary of Human Services.

A police report said a Metropolitan Police officer saw a car showing several potential signs of impaired driving, such as swerving between lanes multiple times and sitting at a green light, near the U.S. Capitol on the evening of Jan. 8. When the officer pulled López at North Capitol and E streets NW, he noticed López’s “red, watery eyes” and a “strong odor of alcoholic beverage.”

López told the officer he had had two drinks — later he said one drink — between 3 and 6:30 p.m. The traffic stop was a little before 7:30 p.m. López failed a field sobriety test, and a subsequent breath test recorded a breath-alcohol content of 0.097. The legal limit in the District is 0.08.

López was charged with driving under the influence and operating a vehicle while impaired. He initially pleaded not guilty when first arraigned. But on Monday, he pleaded guilty under a delayed sentencing agreement and agreed to perform community service.

According to the D.C. Superior Court, if a defendant pleads guilty under a delayed sentencing agreement and abides by whatever terms come with that plea, they can return after six months and “will be allowed to withdraw their guilty plea and the charges will be dismissed.” If they fail to abide by the terms, a harsher sentence would be applied.

In López’s case, sentencing was deferred for a year. He has another court appearance scheduled for Dec. 1, 2026.

The governor’s office did not immediately provide a comment on López’s guilty plea.
